accuracy.reason: Cards 1-4 scope relational client/server behavior to InnoDB tables and deployed SQL mode; constraints, autocommit and redo durability are correctly bounded. No universal isolation, replication or recovery guarantee is offered.

evidence.quote: The transaction and locking behavior in this deck describes InnoDB tables.

mechanisms.reason: Cards 5-6 trace version visibility versus current locking reads, deadlock victim retry, and secondary-to-clustered lookup. Cards 7-8 trace receipt/application lag and backup-plus-log reconstruction. Inspected diagrams preserve these directions and boundaries.

evidence.quote: Receipt and application are different stages; reads can remain old until application catches up.

coherence.reason: All nine objectives are supported in prerequisite order: server, engine, rules, explicit transaction, concurrency, physical index implications, replication, distinct recovery paths and requirement-led synthesis. Basic SQL prerequisites suffice for the locking-read transfer.

evidence.quote: Several successful SQL statements are not automatically one atomic operation.

decisions.reason: Cards 3-9 make configuration verification, protected check/change, bounded retries, key width, index cost, fresh-read routing, safe authority and tested recovery actionable. Choice remains conditional on workload and failure targets.

evidence.quote: Clarify read/write traffic, stale-read tolerance, acknowledged-write loss, write latency and downtime.

clarity.reason: Definitions and the price snapshot example clarify difficult distinctions; schema/ACID/concurrency cards remain dense but usable. Diagram captions correctly explain covering-index exception and backup replay stop point.

evidence.quote: A cycle of transactions waiting for each other's locks.

outcomes.reason: Covers separate SQL server/shared relational joins, workload-owned design, engine role, InnoDB capabilities and finer locks without eliminating waits/deadlocks.

Covers types, all constraints and null cases, deployed version/mode, workflow limits, explicit group transaction rather than autocommit, all ACID properties, delayed-flush risks and external HTTP boundary.

Explains RR first plain-read snapshot and own changes versus current locking reads; safe lock-before-check decrement, failed availability and complete deadlock retry. Covers clustered rows, repeated primary keys, compact-key tradeoff, measured EXPLAIN/index choice and scans/write costs.

Traces source binlog to replica receive/apply, async acknowledged-loss and stale-read risk, safe route/promotion; distinguishes crash recovery, failover and historical recovery. Requires base plus continuous retained logs, stop-before-error and usable timed restores.

Qualifies InnoDB choice by schema/engine/mode, coordinated transactions and retries, measured keys/indexes, connection and transaction limits, lag and write-capacity boundaries, and unknown failure/recovery targets.

sourceChecks.claim: Live inspected MySQL client/server SQL architecture and relational tables; multiple client programs connect to the server rather than requiring in-process file calls.
Live inspected InnoDB introduction and capability table: default engine, transactional recovery, foreign keys and row locking. Other engines differ.

Live inspected SQL-mode abc-to-integer example: nonstrict conversion/warning versus strict error. Followed enforced CHECK documentation: TRUE or UNKNOWN passes, FALSE fails; explicit NOT NULL is separate.

Live inspected START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and default standalone autocommit. Followed InnoDB flush-log setting: default 1 writes and flushes at commit; relaxed settings can lose transactions.

Live inspected Repeatable Read first consistent-read snapshot and different locking statement behavior/range locks. Followed locking reads for latest data and deadlock handling for full transaction reissue and short duration.
Live inspected clustered row storage, secondary primary-key payload and width cost; followed optimization/index guidance on query conditions and write/storage maintenance.

Live inspected default asynchronous source/replica replication and source-write/read-scale distinction; followed replication threads to separate relay-log receipt from SQL application. Previously inspected GTID applied-progress checks support freshness evidence.

Live inspected PITR definition and event-position recovery example: restore an appropriate full backup then replay later binary logs stopping before the unwanted event. Retained continuous history bounds available recovery; tests are an explicit operational requirement.

Live inspected InnoDB feature scope together with index, isolation and replication limits above. The card frames connections, latency and recovery as requirements to verify, not automatic product promises.
